exam_format: Paper-based; two sections: multiple choice and free response. Administered at school in May. AP Studio Art/Drawing: portfolio submission. AP Research/Seminar: academic paper and oral presentation.
exam_price_notes: $98 per exam; $55 for students with fee reductions; +$40 international surcharge

testing_centers.notes: AP exams are administered at school sites in May. Some international testing available at authorized international centers. Students must be enrolled in the AP course or register independently through their school.

id_requirements: School ID or government-issued photo ID required. Name on registration must match ID exactly.
exam_rules: No electronic devices (including phones and smartwatches) permitted during the exam. Approved calculators allowed for some sections (e.g., AP Calculus, AP Statistics, AP Physics). AP Studio Art and AP Research/Seminar are assessed via portfolio or academic paper rather than a timed written exam. All exams are paper-based (multiple choice + free-response) except AP Computer Science Principles (some digital components).
renewal_options: AP scores never expire; once earned, scores are valid indefinitely.

retake_policy.notes: AP exams are offered once per year in May. Students may retake the exam in a subsequent year; there is no same-year retake. Scores from all attempts are reported to colleges unless the student requests score cancellation.

editorial.meta_description: AP English Language and Composition, a College Board exam, assesses rhetorical analysis, evidence, argument, synthesis and style in a 195‑minute test.
editorial.overview: The AP English Language and Composition exam, administered by the College Board, evaluates students' ability to analyze rhetorical situations, assess claims and evidence, organize reasoning, apply style, and produce synthesis, rhetorical analysis, and argumentative essays. It is a paper‑based test delivered in May with multiple‑choice and free‑response sections, and the exam is scored on a 1–5 scale, with many colleges granting credit for scores of 3 or higher.
editorial.who_should_take: High‑school students ready to read college‑level nonfiction and write clear, evidence‑based essays should take this exam. It benefits those seeking college credit or advanced placement in introductory composition courses.
editorial.preparation_strategy: Use AP Classroom Progress Checks after each unit to gauge mastery of rhetorical analysis and writing skills. Practice multiple‑choice questions for speed, then write timed free‑response essays focusing on synthesis, analysis, and argument. Review sample exam questions and scoring guidelines to align your responses with AP expectations.

domain_guidance.summary: Focuses on identifying audience, purpose, and context of a text, and how these elements shape the writer’s choices. Mastery involves recognizing rhetorical appeals and the constraints of the situation.
Centers on assessing the validity and relevance of claims, and the quality of supporting evidence. Students learn to distinguish strong from weak evidence and to evaluate argument credibility.

Involves analyzing how ideas are organized and how reasoning progresses throughout a text. Learners practice tracing logical flow, identifying effective organizational patterns, evaluating paragraph transitions, and assessing whether the overall structure supports the author’s purpose.

Examines the writer’s stylistic choices, including diction, syntax, and rhetorical devices, and how they affect tone and audience perception. Students also consider how word choice shapes voice, how sentence variety influences rhythm, and how figurative language reinforces the argument.

Requires students to combine multiple sources into a cohesive essay, demonstrating synthesis of ideas and evidence while maintaining a clear thesis. They must also organize the essay with logical progression, cite sources appropriately, and ensure each paragraph contributes to the central argument.

Focuses on dissecting nonfiction texts to explain how rhetorical strategies achieve specific effects, requiring close reading and analytical writing. Students practice identifying ethos, pathos, and logos, analyzing how evidence supports claims, and crafting essays that articulate the impact of these strategies on audience perception.

Involves constructing persuasive arguments supported by evidence, with attention to logical structure, style, and audience awareness. Students learn to develop a strong thesis, organize claims coherently, integrate textual evidence, and refine language for maximum persuasiveness.

editorial.exam_day_guidance: Arrive early, bring your admission ticket and photo ID, and have a #2 pencil ready. Manage time across the multiple‑choice and free‑response sections, and review answers if time permits.

faq.question_title: How many sections are on the exam?
faq.answer_text: The AP English Language exam consists of two sections: a multiple‑choice portion and a free‑response portion. The multiple‑choice section tests reading and analysis, while the free‑response section includes synthesis, rhetorical analysis, and argument essays.
A score of 3 on the 1–5 AP scale is considered passing. Scores of 3, 4, or 5 are typically accepted for college credit or placement by most institutions.
The exam lasts 195 minutes, administered in a single day during May. It is a paper‑based test that includes both multiple‑choice and free‑response items officially.

faq.question_title: How much does the AP English Lang exam cost?
faq.answer_text: The standard fee is $98 per exam. Students who qualify for fee reductions pay $55, and an additional $40 international surcharge applies for candidates outside the United States.
